## How to use this handout

::: {.fiche n="0.2" etat="fige"}
Intention : The shared user guide, plus what is specific to this course: the investigation, writing before the answer, the certainty bar, the revision mode. AI transparency statement. [new]
Experience : none
Request :
:::

This course is an **investigation**. Almost every slide asks you to look, write or choose **before** reading the answer.

- The **icon** in front of each title gives the level: **core**, to master; **support**, to consolidate; **further**, to go beyond. A slide without an icon is an example.
- The **writing boxes** keep what you write, in your browser only: you will find it again later on.
- The **certainty bar** asks you, before answering, how sure you are. At the end, the course compares your certainty with your results.
- The last part holds a **revision mode**, to reopen in a day, a week, a month.

::: {.transparence-ia profil="✒️ The equipped Author" coordonnees="F2 · R0 · S0" outil="Claude 5"}
:::

::: {.bilan moment="debut"}
- C1 | Describe before interpreting: separate what I see from what I infer, identification from interpretation
- C2 | Know the reflexes of image reading, and in particular identify the nature of the signal
- C3 | Identify an object with the identification keys: tone, size, shape, texture, pattern, shadow, date
- C4 | Interpret a scene by cross-checking clues, and state a degree of certainty
- C5 | Choose the image or signal suited to a question, and know its limits
- C6 | Turn an interpretation into data: nomenclature, minimum mapping unit, checks
- C7 | Tell a real image from a generated one
:::

## Induction, deduction, abduction {.socle competences="C4"}

::: {.fiche n="1.3" etat="a-revoir"}
Intention : The cognitive process of the investigation. Marc's definitions: induction draws a rule from repeated facts (highly probable, never absolutely certain); deduction draws a conclusion from rules or premises (certain if they are true); abduction puts forward hypotheses to explain an observed fact (no certainty, leads, above all when the fact surprises). Sherlock Holmes's "deduction" is mostly abduction. [V0 feedback: Marc's definitions; the examples form the bundle of clues.] [V1 feedback: the left part given more room and centred vertically; the exercise moves to the next slide, replaced here by the image of the Rosny tower, which illustrates the bundle.]

## Stating your certainty {.socle competences="C4"}

::: {.fiche n="1.7" etat="a-revoir"}
Intention : An interpretation without a degree of confidence is an opinion. Sherman Kent's "words of estimative probability" (CIA, 1964); the IPCC does the same in its reports. Each sentence is completed with a word of certainty, on the image of the radio telescope, still unnamed. [V0 feedback: link with the IPCC; a single certainty, in the sentences.] [V1 feedback: the magnifier on the image.]
Experience : sentences to complete with a word of certainty ("phrases" brick); magnifier; bonus: the IPCC scale
Request :
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="38%"}
In 1964, Sherman Kent, a CIA analyst, proposed matching words and odds:

| Word | Odds |
|---|---|
| Almost certain | about 9 in 10 |
| Probable | about 3 in 4 |
| Possible | about 1 in 2 |
| Unlikely | about 1 in 3 |

[A word of certainty commits you: it tells the reader what risk they take in believing you.]{.a-retenir}
:::
::: {.column width="62%"}
::: {.loupe zoom="3"}
![](images/fast-2016.jpg){height="235" fig-alt="Satellite image of a large silver disc at the bottom of a wooded hollow, with blue-roofed buildings"}
:::

::: {.phrases}
- It is {almost certain|=probable|possible|unlikely} that there are workers on the site : nobody can be seen, but the blue-roofed workers' camp is there.
- It is {=almost certain|=probable|possible|unlikely} that construction is under way : bare earthworks, new tracks, a workers' camp: the clues converge.
- It is {almost certain|probable|possible|=unlikely} that we are in the United States : these sugar-loaf hills and blue roofs rather point to southern China.
- It is {almost certain|probable|possible|=unlikely} that this image comes from an AI : the roads lead somewhere, the shadows are consistent.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.plus titre="The IPCC, too"}
IPCC reports describe the likelihood of an outcome with fixed terms, in italics in the text: *virtually certain* (99-100%), *very likely* (90-100%), *likely* (66-100%), *more likely than not* (over 50%), *about as likely as not* (33-66%), *unlikely* (0-33%), *very unlikely* (0-10%), *exceptionally unlikely* (0-1%). This terminology has been applied consistently since the Fifth Assessment Report (AR5).

[Source: Belgian federal climate portal, climat.be, "Rapports du GIEC" (in French).](https://climat.be/changements-climatiques/changements-observes/rapports-du-giec)
:::

Confirmation bias: we see what we are looking for. [V0 feedback: Colin Powell's portrait (Wikipedia).] [V1 feedback: instead of the archive image, the link to the photos shown that day, on CBS News.]
Experience : visit the site; question: which step of the method was missing?
Request :
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="24%"}
![](images/colin-powell.jpg){height="250" fig-alt="Official portrait of Colin Powell, Secretary of State"}

[Colin Powell, US Secretary of State (official portrait).]{.legende}
:::
::: {.column width="76%"}
On 5 February 2003, at the UN Security Council, **Colin Powell** presents satellite images as proof of chemical weapons in Iraq. The weapons will never be found.

**See:** [the photos shown that day, on the CBS News website](https://www.cbsnews.com/pictures/powells-photos/).

::: {.question}
**Which step of the method was missing?**
:::

::: {.reponse}
Looking for the clue that **contradicts**, and stating the real **certainty**. A truck near a bunker has many possible explanations; the one expected is chosen. This is **confirmation bias**.
:::
:::
::::

- **BD Forêt V2** (IGN, 2007-2018): forests interpreted on colour-infrared photographs, 32 types, no patch under **0.5 ha**.
- **CORINE Land Cover**: Europe's land cover, no patch under **25 ha**.

::: {.question}
**Why do three databases not say the same thing about one place?**
:::

::: {.reponse}
They do not share the same question, the same nomenclature, or the same **minimum mapping unit**. A database is an interpretation, made according to rules.

## What is a forest? {.appui competences="C6"}

::: {.fiche n="2.3" etat="a-revoir"}
Intention : A nomenclature starts with definitions. Students build a definition of forest from three criteria (minimum area, tree height, cover), then find out whether such a definition exists: FAO, UNFCCC (Kyoto), BD Forêt V2, CORINE Land Cover, COMIFAC. Checked thresholds: FAO 0.5 ha, 5 m, 10%; UNFCCC, each country chooses between 0.05 and 1 ha, 2 and 5 m, 10 and 30%; BD Forêt V2 0.5 ha, 5 m, 20 m wide, aligned with FAO; CORINE 25 ha, over 5 m, at least 30%; COMIFAC (Ernst et al., 2010) 5 ha, 5 m, 70%. [V0 feedback: the nomenclature of the course image becomes the definition of forest, suggested by Marc: three series of items to combine.] [V1 feedback: the definitions ran off the slide once opened; they now sit in two columns.]
Experience : build a definition, then compare it with official definitions ("combiner" brick)
Request :
:::

Build **your** definition of a forest: one choice per row. Then see whether it exists.

::: {.combiner}
### Minimum area

- 0.05 ha [kyoto]
- 0.5 ha [fao, kyoto, bdforet]
- 5 ha [comifac]
- 25 ha [clc]

### Tree height

- 2 m [kyoto]
- 5 m [fao, kyoto, bdforet, clc, comifac]
- 15 m []

### Tree cover

- 10% [fao, kyoto, bdforet]
- 30% [kyoto, clc]
- 70% [comifac]

#### fao | FAO (world statistics)

Over 0.5 ha, trees over 5 m, a cover of over 10%.

#### kyoto | Climate (UNFCCC, Kyoto Protocol)

Each country chooses its thresholds within ranges: 0.05 to 1 ha, 2 to 5 m, 10 to 30% cover.

#### bdforet | BD Forêt V2 (IGN, France)

0.5 ha, trees over 5 m, at least 20 m wide; aligned with FAO.

#### clc | CORINE Land Cover

A minimum mapping unit of 25 ha; a forest has trees over 5 m and a cover of at least 30%.

#### comifac | Central African forests (COMIFAC)

At least 70% cover, trees of at least 5 m, a minimum mapping unit of 5 ha.

#### * | No known definition

None of the definitions kept here combines these three choices. Yet there are hundreds: every country, every database, every convention sets its own thresholds. A map of "the" forest always says **which** forest.
:::

## How accurate are experts? {.appui competences="C6 C7"}

::: {.fiche n="2.4" etat="fige"}
Intention : One of Marc's slides on expert accuracy. It starts with "How certain are you of yourself?", voted with a slider: the expected answer is close to 95% (depending on age, progress in a field, tiredness, we do not always agree with ourselves: points developed orally). An expert is considered as such at 95%. Then four categories of accuracy in geographic information production, orders of magnitude given by Marc: expert photo interpreter 95%, expert classification highly variable, machine learning 80 to 85%, neural network 92%. The question on disagreements between interpreters stays. [V0 feedback: replaces "Two interpreters, two maps"; bonus: Colwell, 1952, on the links between military and forest photo interpretation.]

::: {.column width="56%"}
::: {.schema fichier="images/schemas/en/precision.svg" hauteur="250"}
:::

[Orders of magnitude in geographic information production (Marc Poupée).]{.legende}

::: {.question}
**Two interpreters: where do they most often disagree?**
:::

::: {.reponse}
At **boundaries**, on **small objects**, on **cases the rules did not foresee**.
:::

::::

::: {.plus titre="Soldiers and foresters"}
Military and forest photo interpreters have shared a lot: same keys, same methods. R. N. Colwell (US Naval Photographic Interpretation Center), "Relationships Between Military and Forest Photo Interpretation", *Journal of Forestry*, 50 (4), 1952, pp. 271-276. [The paper](https://academic.oup.com/jof/article/50/4/271/4684240)
:::

## Data to teach machines {.appui competences="C7"}

::: {.fiche n="2.5" etat="fige"}
Intention : AI learns from images labelled by people. FLAIR (Garioud, Gonthier, Landrieu, De Wit, Valette, Poupée, Giordano, Wattrelos, NeurIPS 2023): over 20 billion labelled pixels, 817 km² of 20 cm aerial imagery, with satellite time series. The interpreter becomes an annotator. Marc's reflection, kept here and not on the slide: AI takes in labelled data, not data being labelled; the interpreter's decision process is unknown. Including the margin of certainty in training data would be an interesting lead. [V0 feedback: AI learns the errors, not the hesitations; the orthophoto and its labels side by side.]
Experience : look at the image and its labels; question; bonus: the paper
Request :
:::

![](images/flair-ortho.png){height="215" fig-alt="Orthophoto of a small town surrounded by fields"} ![](images/flair-etiquettes.png){height="215" fig-alt="The same area, each pixel coloured by its land cover"}

[The image, and its pixel-by-pixel labels. The **FLAIR** dataset (IGN, 2023): over 20 billion labelled pixels, across 817 km² of 20 cm imagery.]{.legende}

::: {.question}
**Who makes these labels, and what does the machine learn from them?**
:::

::: {.reponse}
Interpreters, pixel by pixel, following rules. The machine learns their final decisions, **errors included**; their hesitations, it never sees.
:::

::: {.plus titre="The FLAIR paper"}
A. Garioud, N. Gonthier, L. Landrieu, A. De Wit, M. Valette, M. Poupée, S. Giordano, B. Wattrelos, "FLAIR: a Country-Scale Land Cover Semantic Segmentation Dataset From Multi-Source Optical Imagery", *NeurIPS 2023, Datasets and Benchmarks*. [The paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.13336) · [the data](https://ignf.github.io/FLAIR/)
:::

::: {.column width="54%"}
An AI maps buildings. Out of 100 random points, an interpreter checks: **90 are right**.

::: {.confiance}
::: {.qcm .serre}
What can be concluded?

- [ ] The map is 90% right, everywhere
    - No: errors may cluster somewhere (dark roofs, dense areas).
- [x] On this territory, about 9 points in 10 are right; we must look at where the errors are
    - Yes: the overall figure is not enough, the distribution of errors class by class is needed.
- [ ] The interpreter is no longer needed
    - No: the interpreter produced the check.
:::

In 2012, an airborne **LiDAR** flies over Angkor. Its laser pulses pass between the leaves and reach the ground: under the forest, streets, ponds and whole districts appear.

::: {.question}
**Why was an aerial photograph not enough?**
:::

::: {.reponse}
It only shows the radiometry of the canopy. The last LiDAR returns bring out the ir/regularities of the ground and the ancient works that go with them.
:::

Explore the image with the magnifier. **Describe** what you see: shapes, colours, sizes, positions. Then, for each element, what it **probably** is, with a word of certainty. You will find this text again at the end.

::: {.observer cle="description-image" invite="I see… ⇒ it is probably…"}
- Large surfaces, apparently flat, from brown to green, edged with dark lines ⇒ **very probably** fields bordered by hedges.
- A line of large pale blocks closing a turquoise body of water ⇒ **very probably** a breakwater and a basin.
- Stringy white patches at sea, far from shore ⇒ **probably** rough water.
- Two grey discs about fifty metres across, a third copper-coloured one, surrounded by long thin shapes ⇒ **probably** domes, one under construction, with cranes.
- Long rectangular volumes, aligned at right angles ⇒ **very probably** industrial buildings.
- Rows of small coloured rectangles on grey ⇒ **almost certainly** cars in car parks.
:::

## Hollow or bump? {.socle competences="C3 C4"}

::: {.fiche n="3.7" etat="fige"}
Intention : The step that deduces the dish's shape (Marc's request): 1. find where the sun is; 2. find a sundial (the tower at the bottom right of the disc and its shadow); 3. deduce the shape: the sun's reflection is on the side opposite the sun, so the dish is concave. On a dome, the reflection would be on the sun's side. The object is finally named: the FAST radio telescope. [V0 feedback: deduction step that was missing after the profile.]
Experience : riddle with clues, with certainty at each clue ("indices" brick)
Request :
:::

::: {.indices image="images/fast-2016.jpg" alt="The large silver disc, its tower and its reflection" confiance="oui" style="--hauteur-indices: 420px"}
- 46,59,13,8 : A sundial: the tower at the bottom right of the disc, and its thin shadow running left, across the disc.
- So the sun is on the right of the image, slightly low: opposite the shadow.
- 34,38,9,11 : The sun's reflection on the disc is up and to the left of the centre: on the side opposite the sun.
- On a bump, the reflection would be on the sun's side; in a hollow, it is on the opposite side.

The disc is **concave**: a hollow 500 m across, set at the bottom of a karst depression. It is the **FAST radio telescope** (Guizhou, China), the largest single-dish antenna in the world, caught by Pléiades on 2 March 2016, at the end of construction.
:::

## The date matters {.appui competences="C3 C5"}

::: {.fiche n="3.8" etat="a-revoir"}
Intention : The date of an image sets what can be seen on it: construction, the season, the tide, the time of day (length and direction of shadows). On the image of the Rosny tower: can the exact time of the shot be known? How? What precaution (the slope)? Bonus: OSINT and chronolocation. [V1 feedback: the Rosny tower image and Marc's questions, instead of the multiple choice.]
Experience : question, then answer; bonus
Request :
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
![](images/tour-rosny.jpg){height="430" fig-alt="Vertical view of a tall tower and its long cast shadow"}
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
The date tells the **state** of a place: a construction site, a season, a time of day.

::: {.question}
**Can the exact time of the shot be known? How would you go about it? What precaution should you take?**
:::

::: {.reponse}
Yes, to within a few minutes: the shadow's **direction** gives the sun's azimuth, its **length** compared with the tower's height gives the sun's elevation; with the place and the date, SunCalc gives the time. Precautions: the real height of the tower; **flat ground** (a slope lengthens or shortens the shadow); the image's north and date.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.plus titre="OSINT and chronolocation"}
**OSINT** (*open source intelligence*) is intelligence drawn from open sources: published images, videos, maps. **Chronolocation** is one of its branches: dating an image from its clues, the length and direction of shadows first. Tools such as [SunCalc](https://www.suncalc.org) give the sun's position for a place, a day, a time; the [Bellingcat](https://www.bellingcat.com) collective publishes its investigations and methods.
:::

## Which key for which question? {.socle competences="C3"}

::: {.fiche n="3.9" etat="a-revoir"}
Intention : A recap of the identification keys, mixed (interleaved practice): three questions, three main keys (shadow, pattern, shape). [V1 feedback: "which main key"; three questions in three columns, including Marc's: a crop type (pattern), an aircraft (shape).]
Experience : three multiple-choice questions
Request :
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.qcm .serre}
A chimney taller than the next block of flats? **Which main key?**

- [ ] Tone
    - No: it tells the material or the lighting.
- [ ] Shape
    - No: seen from above, a chimney is just a disc.
- [x] Shadow
    - Yes: at the same time of day, the longest shadow belongs to the tallest object.
- [ ] Pattern
    - No: it concerns repeated elements.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.qcm .serre}
To estimate a **crop type**?

- [ ] Tone
    - It helps, but it changes with the season.
- [ ] Shape
    - A field often has the same shape, whatever the crop.
- [ ] Shadow
    - No: a crop is low.
- [x] Pattern
    - Yes: rows of vines, trees in staggered rows, tight furrows: the arrangement tells the crop.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.qcm .serre}
To **identify an aircraft**?

- [ ] Tone
    - No: paint varies from one aircraft to another.
- [x] Shape
    - Yes: wingspan, wing sweep, tail: the silhouette tells the model.
- [ ] Shadow
    - It helps for an aircraft in flight, but shape comes first.
- [ ] Pattern
    - No: an aircraft stands alone, or lined up with others.
:::
:::
::::

[Tone and colour, size, shape, texture, pattern, shadow, date: seven keys to say **what** an object is.]{.a-retenir}

::: {.plus titre="The Mississippi meanders"}
:::: {.columns}

![](images/mississippi-meandres.jpg){height="380" fig-alt="Top, an old map of the successive courses of the Mississippi, in colours; bottom, the satellite image of the same place"}
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
In 1944, Harold Fisk mapped the former courses of the Mississippi, each in its own colour: a chronology of meanders. The Landsat 7 image of 22 September 1999 shows, in the same place, their traces in the landscape.

[NASA Earth Observatory, "Mississippi Meanders"](https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/mississippi-meanders-6887/)
:::

## Reasoning step by step {.socle competences="C1 C4"}

::: {.fiche n="4.9" etat="fige"}
Intention : A deduction tree on the Brest roadstead: what is happening inside the red dashes? Each choice is a clue; the path taken stays on screen, like a bundle. First version: the tree will be rebuilt from the answers of Marc's students, and its conclusions validated by him. [new]
Experience : deduction tree ("arbre" brick)
Request :
:::

What is happening inside the **red dashes**? Answer step by step: each answer is a clue.

::: {.arbre image="images/rade-de-brest.jpg" alt="Orthophoto of the Brest roadstead, a red dashed area on the water" style="--hauteur-arbre: 390px"}
### depart | How big are the small white dots? (scale: 200 m)
- A few metres → petits
- Several tens of metres → grands

### grands ! Measure again
With the scale, 200 m is about 126 pixels: a dot of 3 or 4 pixels measures a few metres. Go back one step.

### petits | How are they spread?
- Scattered, fairly evenly spaced → espaces
- Lined up in straight rows → rangees
- Packed in a group, all heading the same way → groupe

### espaces | Do they all point the same way?
- Yes, all the same way → mouillage
- No, at random → flottants

### mouillage ! Hypothesis: a mooring area
Boats on their moorings, all turned by the same current or wind, near the shore. To confirm: a slipway, a club, a harbour nearby? Conclusion to be validated.

### rangees ! Hypothesis: shellfish or seaweed farming
Buoys lined up on longlines. To confirm: sheds on shore, access tracks? Conclusion to be validated.

### groupe ! Hypothesis: a regatta
Sailing boats moving as a fleet. To confirm: wakes, a course mark? Conclusion to be validated.

### flottants ! Hypothesis: floating objects
Buoys, debris or birds. To confirm with a second date. Conclusion to be validated.
:::

## Traps {.appui competences="C2 C4"}

::: {.fiche n="4.10" etat="a-revoir"}
Intention : False friends (a shadow taken for water) and confirmation bias; the counter: look for the clue that contradicts. In conclusion, typical traps: geometric (a shadow stretched by a slope…), radiometric (paint, shadows, moisture…), the wrong nature of the signal (an unexpected colour composite…), and others on the same principle. [V1 feedback: the conclusion on typical traps, with Marc's examples, completed.]
Experience : multiple choice with a certainty bar; list of typical traps
Request :
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.confiance}
::: {.qcm .serre}
A large dark patch at the foot of a tall building, on an image taken late in the afternoon. What is it?

- [ ] A pond, no doubt
    - Too quick: a cast shadow is just as dark, and it has the shape of the building.
- [x] Probably its shadow: check its shape and direction
    - Yes: if the patch extends the building in the direction of the other shadows, it is a shadow.
- [ ] A car park
    - Nothing suggests it: no cars, no markings.
:::
:::

[The counter to confirmation bias: look for the clue that **contradicts** your hypothesis.]{.a-retenir}
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
**Typical traps**

- **Geometric**: a shadow stretched by a slope; a tall building that "leans over"; a mosaic of different times.
- **Radiometric**: paint, shadows, moisture, sun glint, clouds.
- **Signal**: an unexpected colour composite (infrared turning vegetation red); radar read as a photograph.
- **Scale and date**: a badly measured object; a season that changes everything.
- **Reasoning**: a single clue taken as proof.
:::
::::

## What still gives AI away {.socle competences="C7 C3"}

::: {.fiche n="5.5" etat="a-revoir"}
Intention : What remains today: difficult textures (fur, wrinkles), inconsistent blurred backgrounds, simplified high-spatial-frequency structures typical of convolutional networks; repetitive graphic styles and recurring biases. Marc's images: PXL_20261006_182859009 and PXL_20261006_182903643. [V1 feedback: repetitive graphic styles and recurring biases.]
Experience : look at the two images; list of weak points
Request :
:::

![](images/ia-textures-1.jpg){height="205" fig-alt="A dog licks a boy's cheek"} ![](images/ia-textures-2.jpg){height="205" fig-alt="A boy laughs, eyes screwed up"}

The weak points that remain, to look for with a magnifier:

- fine **textures**: fur, hair, wrinkles;
- **blurred backgrounds** whose blur does not follow distance;
- **fine details** (high frequencies), in over-regular motifs: the signature of convolutional networks;
- **repetitive styles**: golden light, smooth skin, a "cinematic" look;
- **recurring biases**: the same typical faces, the same poses, centred compositions.

## The method {.socle competences="C7 C2 C4"}

::: {.fiche n="5.8" etat="a-revoir"}
Intention : The verification method in five steps, from Marc: nature, source, spatio-temporal consistency, physical consistency, certification. [V1 feedback: Marc's five steps and closing sentence.]
Experience : put the steps in order
Request :
:::

::: {.ordre}
Put the verification of an image in order.

1. Nature: which signal? who published it, when, with what metadata?
2. Source: has it circulated before? (reverse image search)
3. Spatio-temporal consistency: the place, the date, the sun, the season
4. Physical consistency: do the keys hold? (shapes, textures, shadows)
5. Certification: conclude with a degree of certainty
:::

[A single clue is generally fragile. Crossing bundles of clues is what reduces uncertainty.]{.a-retenir}

An interpretation note has **four headings**: what I see; what I infer; how sure I am; on what sources, with what limits.

::: {.observer cle="note-image" rappel="description-image" invite="Observations… Interpretations… Certainty… Sources and limits…"}
**Observations.** A rocky coast, a breakwater enclosing a basin, no boats nor room for any, two domes about 50 m across and a third under construction, long buildings, boils offshore, power lines, all at the foot of a cliff.

**Interpretations.** A nuclear power plant by the sea, cooled by sea water (intake in the basin, outfall offshore), with a third reactor under construction.

**Certainty.** Almost certain for the power plant (a bundle of clues); probable for the water circuit (the tunnels cannot be seen).

**Sources and limits.** One orthophoto, one date; the outfall is inferred, not seen.

## The revision programme

::: {.fiche n="7.3" etat="a-revoir"}
Intention : The revision mode, rebuilt: 32 cards written for recall, different from the course questions, asked as a demanding tutor would. They call on several kinds of memory: free recall (write from memory, then compare), recognition (multiple choice), identification on the course images (a frame points at the object), explanation ("why?"), transfer (a new case), correcting a faulty sentence, procedure (putting a method in order). Cards are mixed and interleaved (never two of the same skill in a row); a known card is spaced out (a day, a week, a month), a missed card comes back in the session. At the top, the seven skills: the one being tested lights up; one whose cards are all known turns grey. [V1 feedback: rebuild requested by Marc.]
Experience : "revision" brick, with its cards; the ?revision address opens this slide directly
Request :
:::

Reopen this handout tomorrow, then in a week (`?revision` at the end of the address brings you here). Write **before** you look at the answer: the effort of recall is what fixes the memory.

::: {.revision}
- C1 | Describe before interpreting
- C2 | Reading reflexes and the nature of the signal
- C3 | Identify with the keys
- C4 | Interpret by cross-checking clues, with certainty
- C5 | Choose the suitable image or signal
- C6 | Turn an interpretation into data
- C7 | Tell the real from the generated

### C1 libre

A classmate writes: "The site is a nuclear power plant." Rewrite the sentence, separating what is seen from what is inferred.

---

"I see two domes about 50 m across, a basin closed by a breakwater, boils offshore. I infer, almost certainly, a nuclear power plant cooled by sea water." Observation first; the inference after, with its word of certainty.

### C1 image | images/cambrai-1917.jpg

Without interpreting anything: three observations about this image. Then a single inference, with its word of certainty.

---

Observations: crenellated zigzag lines; ground riddled with small round holes; wide dark bands parallel to the lines. Inference: very probably Great War trenches, under shell holes.

### C1 qcm

Which of these statements is an observation, not an inference?

- [x] Stringy white patches offshore : that is exactly what is seen, with no conclusion drawn.
- [ ] The water is stirred by an outfall : "outfall" is already an explanation.
- [ ] Construction is under way : it is inferred from the cranes and bare earth.

### C1 image | images/centre-equestre.jpg

Describe this image in five elements, without ever naming the place or the activity.

---

Two large areas of pale sand; on one, poles set out in lines; long buildings around a courtyard; a car park with long vehicles; small elongated figures on the sand. If you wrote "horses", you have already interpreted.

### C2 libre

Faced with an unknown image, which questions do you ask **before** any interpretation? At least four.

---

Which place? Which date (and season, time of day)? Which signal: visible, colour infrared, radar, panchromatic, LiDAR? Which scale and resolution? Which source, and is it reliable?

### C2 qcm

On an image, fields and hedges are bright red, water almost black. What do you conclude **first**?

- [x] It is a colour-infrared composite : living vegetation strongly reflects near infrared.
- [ ] The vegetation is diseased : on the contrary, diseased vegetation turns less red.
- [ ] The image is generated : nothing says so, the signal is enough to explain it.

### C2 image | images/baltimore-radar.jpg

What is the signal of this image? What tells you so, and what trap does it set?

---

Radar, multi-date: a particular grain, grey everywhere, colour only where something changed. The trap: reading it as a photograph, and looking for "colours" that are not colours.

### C2 image | images/flamanville-irc-2015.jpg

Why are the fields red on this image? What does someone who fails to notice risk?

---

It is colour infrared: near infrared, strongly reflected by living vegetation, is displayed in red. Someone who misses it takes the signal for a real colour, and concludes wrongly (fields of flowers, pollution…).

### C3 image | images/flamanville.jpg | 53,46,7,17

What are these framed objects? Which keys let you say so, and which one was missing to be sure?

---

Two domes about fifty metres across: size (the scale) and shape (a perfect circle, so human-made). Alone, they remain ambiguous: association (intake, outfall, turbine halls) was needed to conclude they are reactor buildings.

### C3 libre

Name the seven identification keys. For three of them, give an object that key alone almost lets you recognise.

---

Tone and colour, size, shape, texture, pattern, shadow, date. For example: shadow for a pylon or a wind turbine; pattern for a vineyard or an orchard; shape for an aircraft.

### C3 qcm

A conifer and a broadleaf tree, on a vertical photo taken late in the afternoon. Which key tells them apart best?

- [x] Shadow : triangular for the conifer, round for the broadleaf.
- [ ] Size : two trees can be the same height.
- [ ] Tone : it varies with the season and the lighting.

### C3 image | images/fast-2016.jpg | 34,38,9,11

This framed reflection: what does it prove about the disc's shape, and why?

---

The sun is on the right (the tower's shadow runs left); the reflection is on the opposite side. On a bump, it would be on the sun's side: so the disc is concave, a hollow.

### C3 libre

Explain to a classmate, in three sentences, why the cast shadow is often more useful than the object itself on a vertical image.

---

Seen from above, a tall thin object shrinks to a dot. Its shadow, cast by a low sun, draws its side silhouette. Its length gives the height, its direction the position of the sun, hence the time.

### C3 image | images/tour-rosny.jpg

Where does the sun come from on this image? How do you know?

---

Opposite the tower's shadow: the shadow runs one way, the sun is on the other side. Every other shadow in the image must point the same way; if one does not, be wary.

### C4 libre

Induction, deduction, abduction: one sentence for each, and an example taken from an image.

---

Induction draws a rule from repeated cases (the domes seen so far housed reactors). Deduction applies a rule to a case (the image is from April, the rapeseed will be yellow). Abduction offers the best explanation of a fact (a dark patch at the foot of a tower: probably its shadow).

### C4 qcm

"A bright yellow field in spring: perhaps rapeseed." Which reasoning?

- [ ] Induction : no rule is drawn from repeated cases.
- [ ] Deduction : the conclusion is not certain.
- [x] Abduction : the best hypothesis for an observed fact.

### C4 qcm

On Sherman Kent's scale, "probable" means…

- [ ] 9 chances in 10 : that is "almost certain".
- [x] About 3 chances in 4.
- [ ] 1 chance in 2 : that is "possible".

### C4 libre

Why is a single clue fragile? Give an ambiguous object, and what removes the ambiguity.

---

A single clue often has several explanations. A dome can be a planetarium, a silo, a radome: its association with an intake, an outfall and high-voltage lines makes it a reactor. Crossing bundles of clues reduces uncertainty.

### C4 image | images/schemas/en/chronologie.svg

On this diagram, which feature is the most recent? Which rule tells you so?

---

D, the housing estate under construction: it plugs into the motorway, which itself cuts across the railway. What cuts across is younger than what it cuts.

### C4 libre

The riding centre: which associations let you identify it? Why was none of them enough on its own?

---

Sand arenas with jump poles, buildings around a courtyard (stables), long vehicles (horseboxes), figures on the sand (riders). Each alone has other explanations (a sand quarry, a warehouse, a car park); together, only one.

### C5 qcm

To see remains under the forest of Angkor, which data do you choose?

- [x] Airborne LiDAR : its last returns reach the ground, under the canopy.
- [ ] A colour orthophoto : it only sees the forest roof.
- [ ] A radar image : it goes through clouds, not through dense forest.

### C5 libre

A flood, under an overcast sky for three days: which sensor do you choose? Which limit do you accept?

---

Radar: it sees through clouds, day and night, and calm water appears dark. The limit: no colours, a hard reading, possible confusion (roads, radar shadows).

### C5 qcm

To photograph a bank levelled to 30 cm, when should you fly?

- [x] In grazing light, early morning or late evening : the slightest relief casts a shadow.
- [ ] At noon, in full sun : shadows are then at their shortest.
- [ ] Under an overcast sky : with no sun, no shadow.

### C5 libre

Why is the date of an image a limit as much as a piece of information?

---

It tells the state of the place at one moment: a construction site, a season, a tide. But the image only shows that moment: what happened before or after escapes it, and a single date shows no dynamic.

### C6 qcm

CORINE Land Cover (25 ha) and BD Forêt V2 (0.5 ha) give almost the same total forest area. What do you conclude?

- [ ] That they agree : the total says nothing about places.
- [x] Nothing yet : look at where they differ, often on small patches and boundaries.
- [ ] That the finer one is wrong : each answers its own question.

### C6 libre

What is a minimum mapping unit? What happens to a 2 ha copse in CORINE Land Cover, and in BD Forêt V2?

---

The area below which an object is not mapped. In CORINE (25 ha), the copse disappears, merged into the neighbouring class; in BD Forêt V2 (0.5 ha), it is mapped.

### C6 libre

Why can two countries count the same forest differently?

---

Because they do not define it the same way: minimum area, tree height, cover. Under the Kyoto Protocol, each chooses its thresholds (0.05 to 1 ha, 2 to 5 m, 10 to 30%). A map of "the" forest always says which forest.

### C6 qcm

An AI claims 90% right answers on a building map. What do you ask?

- [ ] Nothing : 90% is a good interpreter's level.
- [x] Where the errors are, class by class and area by area.
- [ ] The model's name : it says nothing about the map.

### C7 libre

Name five clues that still give a generated image away.

---

Failed fine textures (fur, wrinkles), inconsistent blurred backgrounds, over-regular fine details, impossible physics (rivers crossing ridges, multiple lighting), missing emotion, graphic styles and biases that keep coming back.

### C7 image | images/ia-2024-relief-1.jpg

What gives this image away? Name the key that tells you so.

---

Rivers that do not follow valleys and a crumpled relief, with no erosion logic: physical consistency, the key of relief and site.

### C7 libre

The five steps of verifying an image, in order, with a word for each.

---

Nature (the signal, the publication, the metadata); source (has it circulated before?); spatio-temporal consistency (the place, the date, the sun); physical consistency (do the keys hold?); certification (conclude with a degree of certainty).

### C7 qcm

An unusual image is circulating on social media. Your first reflex?

- [x] Look for its source and date : where does it come from, has it circulated before?
- [ ] Look for artefacts : useful, but after the source.
- [ ] Conclude it is generated : an unusual image can be real.
:::
